BODY:
A clean vintage Gibson LG-2 has a published reference of $3,500 to $8,500 across its original eras, while the LG-0, LG-1 and LG-3 need their own model ranges. These are excellent-condition, original-case references from the 2025 price guide, reviewed against completed sales as of October 2026. I use the model and repair history to narrow the comparison.

If the model is uncertain, start with my [Gibson LG identification and construction guide](/post/joesvintageguitarsaz-com-identify-gibson-lg-series/). A sunburst top alone doesn't distinguish an LG-1 from an LG-2, and the price table assumes that identification has already been resolved.

The LG-0, LG-1 and LG-3 rows use broad model envelopes because the available completed comparisons don't justify narrow annual estimates.

Each range assumes an all-original guitar in excellent condition, structurally sound and accompanied by its original case. A quality refret is accepted maintenance under my grading approach, although it removes museum-quality status. Refinished, repaired or substantially altered instruments need a separate comparison.

## What These References Can Tell You

The table gives an owner a starting range and a way to sort the evidence. It doesn't turn an uncertain model, repaired top or incomplete parts description into an excellent original guitar. A guitar can be a useful instrument and still belong outside the clean reference.

I separate the published reference from the completed-sale checks. The reference guide describes an ideal condition category; the transactions show what particular instruments with particular histories brought. Some of the inspected transactions have refinishes, replaced bridges, repaired cracks, added pickups or newer cases.

Those differences are retained in the research behind this page. I don't average a repaired instrument into a clean band and then describe the result as an original-condition market. The ranges remain explicitly dated published references.

### Broad Model Ranges Need A Second Step

The LG-0, LG-1 and LG-3 each span more than one construction period. Their combined envelopes let an owner find the correct model without pretending that the evidence supports a different price for every calendar year. The next step is to match the guitar's actual features and condition.

The LG-1 and LG-3 completed comparisons reviewed here are concentrated in the 1950s. They don't establish separate wartime sale bands. An early example should receive an individual assessment instead of being placed at the top of the range simply because its date is older.

The LG-2 evidence permits a more useful split between the spruce-top Banner period, early postwar examples and later production. Even there, the same era reference appears in several annual rows. Year-by-year coverage and year-specific transaction samples are different things.

## Choosing The Correct LG Model

I begin an appraisal with the model designation and the evidence supporting it. An old receipt, a family description and a seller's listing title can help, but they can also repeat a mistake. A guitar described as an LG-2 for years can still need closer examination.

The published site guide explains the construction distinctions. Here, the practical consequence is simple: don't borrow another model's range because the two guitars look similar from the front. The LG-0, LG-1, LG-2 and LG-3 have separate reference categories.

[IMAGE 2]

### The LG-0

The LG-0 occupies the lowest broad reference in this group. That doesn't mean every inexpensive-looking Gibson is an LG-0, or that an owner's instrument should be assigned the bottom figure without an inspection. Bridge work, playability and condition can change the comparison considerably.

The site's chronology and the published guide begin the model in 1958. Some marketplace category titles use an earlier start date. I retain the supported site date instead of allowing a marketplace heading to create extra production years.

The site's general description calls the LG-0 all-mahogany, while one inspected later completed listing describes a spruce top. I don't resolve that discrepancy from the listing title or extend either description to every year. A later guitar with uncertain wood or model identity needs a closer appraisal.

### The LG-1

An LG-1 can resemble an LG-2 closely enough that owners compare the wrong completed listings. The broad LG-1 reference here remains separate, even where both instruments share a sunburst finish. It covers original-condition guitars rather than every repaired student-model acoustic offered under the name.

A changed bridge or a pickup installation should be described directly. Calling an instrument a good player doesn't answer whether its finish, bridge and internal structure match the reference condition. I want those details before narrowing a price.

### The LG-2 And LG-3

The LG-2's sunburst appearance and the LG-3's natural top provide familiar visual context, but a photograph doesn't settle everything an appraisal needs. I still need the condition and work history. An attractive top can sit above repaired braces or a changed bridge plate.

The LG-3 range is deliberately broad across the original run. I haven't applied a fixed percentage premium to the LG-2 or assumed that any natural-finish guitar is worth more. The model, era and condition have to support that conclusion.

[IMAGE 3]

## Repairs That Change The Comparison

Old acoustics often arrive with maintenance records, replacement parts or work whose history is unknown. I separate those situations from the clean reference instead of giving every repair the same deduction. The extent and quality of the work determine which other guitars make useful comparisons.

A disclosed repair is easier to assess than a vague statement that a guitar was serviced. A receipt naming a neck reset, bridge replacement or brace repair helps explain the instrument's present condition. It also prevents unrelated work from being grouped together.

### Bridges And The Surrounding Top

A bridge holds the strings at the soundboard, and a replacement affects both the instrument's setup and its originality description. A well-made replacement may be a sensible repair. It still isn't the same evidence as an untouched original bridge.

I don't recommend replacing a bridge simply to prepare an instrument for an appraisal. Photograph the guitar as it stands and provide any repair information you have. A specialist can then assess whether work is needed and how the current condition compares with the reference.

On examples associated with plastic bridges, a wood replacement may be part of the instrument's known history. That history should stay with the guitar. The correct value comparison describes the actual bridge rather than treating all examples from the same year as identical.

[IMAGE 4]

### Neck Work And Playability

A neck reset changes the neck's seating angle so the guitar can be set up properly. A documented reset and an instrument that still needs one present different situations to a buyer. I don't assign a universal deduction to the phrase alone.

Frets are another separate question. Under this site's grading approach, a quality refret preserves the all-original classification of an otherwise original guitar, but it removes museum-quality status. Neck reshaping, a broken headstock and changed hardware need their own descriptions.

### Cracks, Braces And Bridge Plates

A repaired crack, a missing brace and a changed bridge plate aren't interchangeable repairs. The bridge plate is the reinforcement beneath the bridge inside the body. Its condition belongs in an acoustic appraisal even when the outside photographs look clean.

I use repair records and appropriate photographs to understand the work. I don't assume that a small visible line is harmless, or that every repaired crack has the same price effect. The clean table isn't a substitute for that assessment.

[IMAGE 5]

## Original Finish, Cases And Added Pickups

An original finish, an overspray and a full refinish need separate descriptions. Overspray means additional finish applied over an existing surface. It can appear in a completed listing alongside other repairs, so I don't isolate a discount without understanding the whole guitar.

The ranges assume the original case. A newer case may protect an instrument well, but it doesn't satisfy that condition assumption. A seller calling a case vintage also doesn't establish that it left the factory with that guitar.

An added pickup can be useful to a working musician. Its installation may involve a changed endpin, a jack or other alterations that belong in the appraisal record. I don't turn that practical usefulness into an automatic collector premium.

Keep removed original parts and any dated receipts together with the guitar. Those items can explain what changed even when they aren't currently installed. Don't reinstall parts merely to make the instrument resemble a reference photograph.

## Reading The Market Without Mixing Categories

A completed price is different from an advertised price. The completed transaction history supplies the realized figure used in this research, while the corresponding listing supplies its year and condition description. I inspect both because marketplace categories can contain misidentified instruments.

An asking price can show what a seller hopes to receive, but it doesn't establish what another buyer paid. I haven't used current asking listings to manufacture higher bands. I also haven't presented any researched transaction as my own purchase or sale.

The dates on the research stay attached to the figures. A 2025 published reference reviewed in October 2026 remains a 2025 reference. It isn't a fresh 2026 market survey simply because this page was updated.

I don't promise an investment return from these ranges. Ownership costs, future repair needs and the time needed to find a buyer all affect the outcome. The useful question is how the actual guitar compares with documented instruments today.

## Preparing An Individual Appraisal

Start with clear photographs of the front, back, headstock, bridge and any known repairs. Include the case and any paperwork that explains the guitar's history. If a date or model name came from a family member rather than a documented inspection, say so.

You don't need to fill in uncertain details before contacting me. An honest unknown is more useful than a confident guess that directs the appraisal toward the wrong model. I can begin with the photographs and explain what additional information would narrow the comparison.

I buy vintage guitars nationwide from my shop in Mesa, Arizona. A [free guitar appraisal](/free-appraisal/) can establish the next step, and my [Gibson selling information](/sell-my-gibson-guitar/) explains the purchase process. The price references here help frame that conversation; the offer depends on the individual instrument.

mainEntity.name: How Much Is A Vintage Gibson LG-2 Worth?

acceptedAnswer.text: The published clean reference is $6,500 to $8,500 for a spruce-top Banner LG-2, $5,500 to $7,500 for 1946 to 1949, and a combined $3,500 to $6,500 for 1950 to 1962. Those are 2025 references reviewed against completed sales as of October 2026, assuming excellent original condition and the original case. Repairs and changed parts need separate comparisons.

mainEntity.name: Do Identical Rows Mean Every Year Sells For The Same Amount?

acceptedAnswer.text: No. Repeated rows identify a shared model or era reference, not a separate sale sample for that year. The LG-0, LG-1 and LG-3 ranges combine several published eras. The exact year, bridge, repairs and case help place an individual guitar within or outside that broad reference.

mainEntity.name: Can An LG-1 Use The LG-2 Price Range?

acceptedAnswer.text: No. Their similar outline and sunburst finish don't make them the same model. I establish the model before choosing a price reference. The separate identification guide explains the construction differences.

mainEntity.name: Does A Replaced Plastic Bridge Make An LG Worthless?

acceptedAnswer.text: No. A well-fitted wood bridge can make an instrument useful to a player, but it changes the originality description. I assess the replacement, surrounding top and disclosed work together instead of applying an automatic percentage.

mainEntity.name: Are There Original LG Models From 1979 In These Tables?

acceptedAnswer.text: These tables stop at each model's published original-run endpoint. They don't extend discontinued models to 1979 or treat a later B-25 as an LG-2. An uncertain label needs identification before a value comparison.

mainEntity.name: Does A Refret Change The Originality Category?

acceptedAnswer.text: A quality refret preserves the all-original classification of an otherwise original guitar under this site's grading approach. It removes museum-quality status. A replaced bridge, altered bracing or repaired neck is a separate condition issue.
